Table 7. Paper attribution for Approach: Agent reasoning & planning

Reasoning paradigms. ReAct reasoning interleaves reasoning, tool action,
and observation, making it a natural fit for interactive security tasks
where each command changes what the agent knows next ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [De Santis et
al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Thanh et
al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Loevenich et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84)). Rather than producing a single final answer from a
static prompt, these agents repeatedly decide what to inspect, execute,
or query. Wu et al.’s AutoPT ([Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22)), for
example, frames web penetration testing as an iterative process in which
the agent observes tool feedback and then chooses the next testing
action. The same pattern appears in benchmark-style agent settings such
as BountyBench ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)), where code
inspection, command execution, and final vulnerability handling are all
part of the action-observation loop.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) makes intermediate reasoning explicit, usually by
asking the LLM to decompose the problem, compare evidence, or justify a
next step before acting ([Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Hmimou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Jiao et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). This paradigm is
especially visible when the agent must translate noisy observations into
a plausible security interpretation. Ginige et al.’s
AutoPentester ([Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)) uses CoT-style
reasoning in its strategy analysis stage to interpret previous
penetration-testing results and choose subsequent attack strategies.
Wang et al.’s PTFusion ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83)) uses
preference-based CoT prompting to align heterogeneous
penetration-testing tool outputs with the current strategic plan.

Reflection / self-critique gives the agent an explicit opportunity to
assess its own intermediate products, failed attempts, or candidate
findings before continuing ([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Gu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). The role of reflection varies by task.
In Chen et al.’s ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)),
reflection is tied to exploration: the agent reconsiders visited binary
locations and candidate bug evidence before deciding where to inspect
next. In Dai et al.’s RefPentester ([Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86)),
reflection has a more operational role, turning failed
penetration-testing attempts into guidance for later actions.

Reflexion is a narrower pattern in which feedback from previous attempts
is converted into reusable verbal guidance for future trials ([Dai et
al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)).
Its main value is continuity across attempts: the agent does not merely
observe failure, but writes down a lesson that changes later behavior.
This is closely aligned with self-reflective penetration testing, where
the same class of mistake can otherwise recur across multiple stages.

Prompt chaining separates a complex task into a sequence of prompts,
each responsible for a narrower subproblem ([Wael et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84)). Few-shot prompting
instead provides examples inside the prompt so that the model can
imitate the desired analysis pattern or output form ([Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Schüring et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Zambare et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Rigaki et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib81); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). These two techniques
address different forms of task complexity: prompt chains control
workflow order, while few-shot examples calibrate local reasoning
behavior. Kim et al.’s AutoRestTest ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)), for
instance, uses example-guided generation to help produce API inputs that
respect parameter semantics and constraints.

Self-debug / self-repair appears when the agent generates an artifact,
tests or checks it, and then revises the artifact based on feedback
([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25);
[Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40);
[Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Abramovich et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Sharanarthi and
Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Bouzenia et
al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). Bouzenia et al.’s
RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87)) illustrates the repair
side: the agent searches for repair ingredients, proposes a fix, and
uses validation feedback to revise its candidate patch. Liu et al.’s
PropertyGPT ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)) follows a similar loop for
formal properties, using compiler, static-analysis, and prover feedback
to revise generated specifications.

Least-to-most task decomposition breaks a large security objective into
smaller subtasks or stages before solving them ([Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Kim et
al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Lan and
Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Loevenich and Lopes,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Wael et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Mei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et

strategy separate from command-level execution.

Hypothesis-driven reasoning starts from possible vulnerabilities, attack
paths, causes, or explanations and then seeks evidence to support or
reject them ([Saheed and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [De Santis et
al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Aldaihan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Qayyum et al.,

2025b](#bib.bib68); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et al.,

2025a](#bib.bib99); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Adler et
al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Deng et
al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)).
In RepoAudit, Guo et al. ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88)) use repository
exploration and validation to move from suspected data-flow facts toward
actionable bug reports. In PropertyGPT, Liu et al. ([Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82)) use formal checking to determine whether generated
properties are compilable, appropriate, and verifiable.

Graph-based reasoning / attack graph construction is important for tasks
whose logic is relational, multi-hop, or path-dependent ([Pendyala et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18)). Graph
structures can represent preconditions, dependencies, attack steps, or
environment states, giving the agent a more explicit reasoning substrate
than a flat prompt.

Unspecified reasoning paradigm denotes papers that do not name or
provide enough procedural evidence for a particular reasoning
paradigm ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47); [Mohammadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Honnalli and
Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Shah and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Chen et
al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Rigaki et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib73); [Bianou and Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Loevenich
et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). We do not infer ReAct or chain-of-thought
from generic iteration, tool use, or multi-step execution alone;
accordingly, “Unspecified” means that the paradigm is under-reported,
not that the agent performs no reasoning.

Planning strategies. Planning strategies capture how an agent plans. A
paper can assign a named Planner agent without describing a specific
planning strategy (e.g., a brief one-line mention of “planning” inside a
larger pipeline), and a paper can plan dynamically without ever naming a
distinct Planner role (e.g., a single ReAct-style loop that revises its
next action after every observation). The two tags therefore overlap
substantially but are not interchangeable, and their totals should not
be read as describing the same set of papers. Dynamic / reactive
planning is the dominant planning style: agents revise their next steps
according to new observations, failed attempts, tool output, or
environment changes ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Luo et al.,

al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Zhang et

2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Gu et al.,

2025](#bib.bib92); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Loevenich et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib43); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib65); [Rigaki et al., 2024a](#bib.bib73); [Huang and Zhu,
2024](#bib.bib75); [Bianou and Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). The important feature is not merely
iteration, but contingency: the next plan depends on what the agent just
learned. ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)) chooses new
binary-analysis targets based on its current exploration context,
whereas RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87)) changes repair
behavior after tests or validation expose problems with a candidate
patch. RedAgent ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85)) dynamically selects
refinement actions based on real-time responses from the target model,
and the ReAct agents benchmarked in JITVUL ([Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)) and Agent Security Bench ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8)) inherit the same thought-action-observation
contingency from their underlying ReAct paradigm.

Hierarchical task decomposition separates high-level objectives from
lower-level execution choices ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36);
[Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83);
[Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Kim et
al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Qayyum et
al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Meruga, 2025](#bib.bib60); [Sharanarthi and
Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Weber
et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Loevenich et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94);
[Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). Zhu et al.’s HPTSA ([Zhu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)) is a clear example: a planning agent analyzes
the target and launches specialized subagents for exploitation subtasks.
RefPentester ([Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86)) uses a staged
penetration-testing structure, letting the current stage constrain which
tactical actions are reasonable. The NVIDIA CVE-triage system of
ZeMicheal et al. ([Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)) follows the same
pattern at the task level: a Plan-and-Execute-style LLM planner first
decomposes each CVE into a context-sensitive checklist, which is then
executed step by step.

Backtracking on failure appears when the agent returns to an earlier
choice, abandons a weak path, or retries from a different branch after
evidence does not support the current plan ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58)). ClearAgent ([Chen et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)) provides a compact example at the analysis
level, revising its exploration direction when the current binary path
does not substantiate a candidate vulnerability.

Unspecified planning strategy denotes papers that mention planning only
in passing, or not at all, without enough procedural detail to classify
the planning behavior as dynamic/reactive, hierarchical, or backtracking
([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Jie et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Wael et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Sheikhi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Jiao et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51); [Shah and Madisetti,
2025](#bib.bib67); [Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). As with
unspecified reasoning paradigms, this label reflects under-reporting
rather than the absence of any planning; we introduce it as a fourth
planning strategy so that under-specified papers are marked explicitly
instead of silently contributing to the denominator without a tag.

Decision-making uncertainty. Confidence-based branching lets the agent
choose different actions depending on the strength of evidence,
estimated risk, or confidence in an intermediate finding ([Rigaki et
al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Chen et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib13); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Aldaihan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51)). PTFusion ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83))
represents this idea at the planning level by using context-aware
knowledge fusion and executed actions to guide more precise next
commands.

Majority voting handles uncertainty by comparing outputs from multiple
agents and selecting the most supported answer ([Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60)). This pattern is most natural when the task admits
plausible disagreement, such as smart-contract vulnerability
classification or ambiguous defensive decisions. In these settings, the
system treats disagreement itself as useful evidence rather than
assuming that a single generation is authoritative.

Human-in-the-loop checkpoints reserve key decisions for human approval,
verification, or guidance ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Sheikhi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Zemicheal et
al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). This is a practical response to uncertainty and
risk: the agent may gather evidence, rank hypotheses, or draft a
recommendation, while a human analyst validates the finding before a
sensitive action is taken. In Sheikhi et al.’s Cognitive SOC ([Sheikhi
et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)), this boundary is visible in the
analyst-facing narrative: the agent organizes evidence and explanation,
but the human remains the decision maker for security-operation
response.

#### 6.2.5. Agent action space

The security capability of an agent is often determined less by the
language model alone than by what the model is allowed to inspect,
execute, query, and validate through tools. The agent action space
describes the external operations that an LLM-based security agent can
invoke after reasoning about a task. In this survey, actions range from
conventional software-analysis utilities to security platforms,
multi-agent coordination mechanisms, and human-facing review steps, as
summarized in
Table [8](#S6.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 6.2.5. Agent action space ‣ 6.2. Survey Result: Approach ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment").

Static analysis tools Dynamic analysis tools Code execution &
environment Information retrieval tools Security-specific platforms
Inter-agent communication Human interaction Year Paper Linters and
pattern matchers (15%) Data- flow/ taint analyzers (5%) Symbolic
execution engines (2%) Formal verification tools (5%) Binary analysis
frameworks (6%) Fuzzers (4%) Debuggers (4%) Execution sandboxes (17%)

Table 8. Paper attribution for Approach: Agent action space

Static analysis tools. Linters and pattern matchers give agents
lightweight static checks over source code, configuration files,
vulnerability templates, and suspicious code idioms ([Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Liu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70);
[Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Jie
et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). These actions usually serve as a first
filter: they point the agent toward likely relevant regions before
deeper reasoning begins. Data-flow/taint analyzers go further by
exposing how values move through a program ([Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Chen et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88)). Guo et al.’s RepoAudit ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88)) uses demand-driven data-flow evidence and validation
to decide whether a suspected bug is feasible along a program path.

Symbolic execution is used to reason about feasible paths and path
conditions ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29)), while formal verification tools checks the
generated or retrieved properties against the precise semantic
requirements ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)). Liu et al.’s
PropertyGPT ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)) generates smart-contract
properties, but the workflow does not stop at generation. It uses
compilation, static analysis, ranking, and a prover to determine whether
the properties are usable for formal verification.

Binary analysis frameworks support reverse engineering and vulnerability
detection when source code is unavailable ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Adler et
al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)). Chen et al.’s
ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)) shows how this action
class changes the role of the LLM. The agent interacts with
binary-analysis interfaces, inspects functions and control-flow
structures, and attempts to validate candidate bugs, so binary
understanding is mediated through analysis actions rather than
unconstrained text generation.

Dynamic analysis tools. Fuzzers let agents generate or mutate inputs to
expose crashes, protocol violations, or hidden vulnerability conditions
([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Yu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88)). Debuggers
give agents a way to inspect intermediate execution states, crashes, and
binary behavior ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Sharanarthi
and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70)).

Execution sandboxes provide controlled environments for running risky
commands, malware-like behaviors, exploit attempts, or benchmark tasks
([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25);
[Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100); [Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Segireddy,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Xenos et al.,
2025](#bib.bib66); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). In BountyBench
([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)), sandboxed environments are central
to assessing agents that must inspect code, exploit vulnerabilities, and
produce patches in realistic targets. Network traffic analysers extend
dynamic observation to packets, flows, IDS evidence, and protocol
behavior ([Saheed and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [De Santis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Eilertsen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)).

Code execution & environment. Compilers / interpreters enable agents to
build, run, and check generated code or specifications ([Luo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib11); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Adler et
al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88)). REPL / shell execution gives the agent direct
command-level access to a target or analysis environment ([Pendyala et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib65); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84)). Containerised environments isolate vulnerable
systems, reproduce experiments, and standardize execution contexts
([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25);
[Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30);
[Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Kluge
et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Adler et
al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Zemicheal et
al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). Shen et al.’s PentestAgent ([Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77)) uses this kind of controlled setting to support
end-to-end penetration-testing workflows, where reconnaissance,
vulnerability analysis, and exploitation must be assessed against
concrete targets. Browser / web automation appears in web exploitation,
prompt-injection assessment, and UI-driven security tasks ([Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Debenedetti et
al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)).

Information retrieval tools. Code search lets agents locate functions,
dependencies, vulnerable files, proof targets, exploit-relevant
snippets, or repair ingredients ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Zhang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Happe et
al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Schüring et
al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Bouzenia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib87); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Zemicheal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). Bouzenia et al.’s
RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87)), for example, searches
the codebase for repair ingredients before constructing and validating
candidate patches. Documentation retrieval covers API references, tool
manuals, exploit writeups, vulnerability reports, cloud documentation,
protocol standards, and remediation guidance ([Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Loevenich
and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18);
[Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31);
[Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chen
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45);
[Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Shah and Madisetti,
2025](#bib.bib67); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Zemicheal et
al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Bianou and
Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Eberhardt
and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). Vector store / RAG retrieval gives
agents a more targeted retrieval action over embedded corpora or
knowledge bases ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Gu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Lan and
Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8);
[Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20);
[Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24);
[De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61);
[Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Sharanarthi and Polineni,
2025](#bib.bib70); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Loevenich et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib43); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). The
difference is visible in PropertyGPT: Liu et al. ([Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82)) retrieve similar human-written smart-contract
properties from a vector database and use them as references for
generating new formal properties. Dai et al.’s RefPentester ([Dai et
al., 2025](#bib.bib86)) applies the same general idea to penetration
testing, retrieving stage-relevant knowledge before choosing later
actions.

Security-specific platforms. CTF platforms provide controlled
exploitation, reverse-engineering, and challenge-solving environments
([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Wu et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Ayzenshteyn
et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Abramovich
et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Zou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). Penetration testing
frameworks embed agents into offensive-security workflows and toolchains
([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26);
[Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83);
[Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib13); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Mei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Geng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Huang and Zhu,
2024](#bib.bib75); [Bianou and Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84)). Vulnerability
scanners appear as actions or baselines that agents invoke, interpret,
or coordinate with ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Segireddy,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89)). In these offensive settings, the agent’s action
space resembles a security practitioner’s toolbelt: scan, enumerate,
exploit, validate, and report.

SIEM / SOAR integration places agents in security-operation workflows
for alert investigation, evidence synthesis, triage, and response
support ([Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Zambare et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib93)). Sheikhi et al.’s Cognitive SOC ([Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)) is a representative defensive example: agents enrich
alerts, reason over evidence, and generate analyst-facing narratives.
MITRE ATT&CK integration gives agents a shared language for tactics,
techniques, and attack-chain reasoning ([Rigaki et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Sheikhi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Ismail et
al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Bianou
and Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76)). Loevenich et al. ([Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42)) connect CTI, CVEs, and ATT&CK-style tactics through
cybersecurity knowledge graphs to support autonomous cyber defense.

Cloud / IaC platform tools support cloud defense, infrastructure policy,
IaC vulnerability analysis, and privilege-escalation workflows ([Zhou et
al., 2026](#bib.bib91); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57);
[Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72);
[Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62);
[Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). Cyber range / network simulation
environments provide controlled networks for assessing attack, defense,
and autonomous cyber operations ([Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Qin
et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge
et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi
et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43);
[Rigaki et al., 2024a](#bib.bib73); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81);
[Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). Asset search / OSINT platforms
connect agents to internet-exposed asset discovery and vulnerability
assessment ([Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89)). Together, these platform
actions show that security agents are often embedded in domain
infrastructures, not merely attached to generic programming tools.

Inter-agent communication. Message passing between agents lets
specialized agents exchange intermediate findings, divide labor, and
coordinate multi-step workflows ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Wu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Loevenich and
Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Qayyum et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59); [Meruga, 2025](#bib.bib60); [Sharanarthi and
Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Zambare
et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51)). This is common when no single agent owns the entire
task, such as incident correlation, multi-stage penetration testing, or
collaborative vulnerability analysis. Voting / aggregation protocols
combine multiple judgments to reduce single-agent errors or resolve
disagreement ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)). Blockchain consensus / audit trail appears as a
stronger accountability mechanism in one multi-LLM network, where agent
proposals and decisions are recorded and checked through consensus ([Luo
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5)). These communication actions matter because
security work often requires defensible coordination, not just
individual prediction.

Human interaction. Querying human expert appears when the agent
explicitly asks a human for clarification, guidance, or execution
support ([Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). Deng et al.’s
PentestGPT ([Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)) reflects this interactive
design: the human can guide the penetration-testing loop and may execute
or validate steps that the agent proposes. Findings for human review is
broader, covering reports, alerts, explanations, remediation
recommendations, and analyst-facing summaries ([Saheed and Chukwuere,
2026](#bib.bib19); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Aldaihan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)).

Mixed topology: sequential stages, parallel dispatch, and iterative
update  
Sequential stage: curriculum orders tasks from easier to harder targets
$`\downarrow`$ Sequential stage: scheduler selects the current
vulnerability task $`\downarrow`$ Parallel dispatch inside the selected
task dispatcher $`\rightarrow`$ planner agent $`\rightarrow`$ attack
plan and task split dispatcher $`\rightarrow`$ recon agent
$`\rightarrow`$ target facts and exposed services dispatcher
$`\rightarrow`$ exploit agent $`\rightarrow`$ candidate exploit attempts
$`\downarrow`$ Sequential stage: merge observations and update task
state $`\downarrow`$ Iterative point: if the attempt fails or new
evidence appears, retrieve experience and return to the scheduler;
otherwise advance to the next curriculum task.

Figure 3. CurriculumPT workflow.

#### 6.2.6. Agent workflow & orchestration

Agent workflow and orchestration describe how an LLM agent organizes
work over time, divides responsibilities among modules or agents, and
decides where human users enter the loop.

summarizes the workflow topologies, coordination patterns, and forms of
human involvement identified in the surveyed systems.

Workflow topology. Workflow topology captures the structural pattern of
the agent process. A sequential pipeline is the most basic form: the
agent progresses through ordered stages such as collecting context,
analyzing evidence, planning a response, executing commands, and
reporting findings. For example, PentestGPT follows a staged
penetration-testing workflow in which high-level reasoning, task
generation, parsing of tool outputs, and next-step selection are
connected in a serial process ([Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)).

Parallel dispatch is used when different agents, tools, or subtasks can
run concurrently and then merge their results ([Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Hmimou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Qayyum et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59); [Meruga, 2025](#bib.bib60); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Zambare et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Loevenich et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib94); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). Parallelism is
useful when the target has multiple independent surfaces, such as
several APIs, hosts, logs, or vulnerability hypotheses. Debate and
discussion are a related but more deliberative form of topology: agents
exchange competing judgments before a final decision is made ([Luo et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95); [Wu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67)).

Iterative loops are used when the agent must repeatedly act, observe,
and revise its state. Such loops appear throughout the surveyed systems
([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5);
[Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Saheed and Chukwuere,

A mixed topology can combine several of these structures. As shown in
Figure [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 6.2.5. Agent action space ‣ 6.2. Survey Result: Approach ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment"),
CurriculumPT ([Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37)) provides such an example:
the overall curriculum proceeds sequentially from easier to harder
penetration-testing tasks; within a selected task, work can be
dispatched to specialized planning, reconnaissance, and exploitation
components; and the workflow iterates by storing successful strategies
and reusing experience in later tasks.

Agent roles. Agent roles describe the functional responsibilities
assigned inside the workflow. Planner, analyst, and executor roles form
the common backbone of agent workflows. A paper is tagged with a Planner
role when it names or describes a component responsible for producing a
plan, independent of which planning strategy that component uses; the
two tags are related but answer different questions, and a paper need
not carry both.

More specialized roles encode security-domain labor. Exploit developer
roles generate or refine attack steps ([Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Bianou and Batogna,
2024](#bib.bib76)), whereas patch generator roles produce fixes or
remediation artifacts ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Yu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). Verifier / tester roles run tests, validate
exploit success, check generated properties, or reduce false positives
([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Wu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100);
[Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Ma
et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). Reporter
roles convert evidence into human-readable findings, incident
narratives, or remediation summaries ([Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3);
[Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). Critic /
judge roles provide a second opinion or quality filter ([Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)), and
orchestrator roles coordinate subagents, maintain global state, or
assign subtasks ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Aldaihan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31); [Geng et al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70);
[Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Wu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94);
[Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)).

For example, in RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87)), the
agent must search for repair ingredients, propose a patch, execute
validation, and revise after feedback. In PropertyGPT ([Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82)), generation is paired with verification: the system
generates formal properties for smart contracts, then checks whether
they compile, fit the target, and can be verified.

HITL integration. Fully autonomous workflows let the agent proceed
without routine human intervention, which is common in benchmarked
penetration testing, cyber-defense simulation, vulnerability scanning,
repair, and analysis pipelines ([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Saheed
and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23);
[Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26);
[Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Wang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Jie et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [De Santis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Ayzenshteyn et
al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Samari et
al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97);
[Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99);
[Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14);
[Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62);
[Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Bianou and Batogna,
2024](#bib.bib76); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)).
Human-on-the-loop workflows keep the system mostly autonomous while
allowing analysts to monitor, review, or approve high-level outcomes
([Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Schüring et
al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Loevenich et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). Human-in-the-loop workflows require human
input at particular decision points, such as executing commands,
providing clarifications, or approving uncertain actions ([Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Adler et al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78)). Interactive or collaborative workflows go further by
treating the human as a continuing collaborator rather than only an
approver ([Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Sharanarthi and Polineni,
2025](#bib.bib70); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). Deng et al.’s
PentestGPT ([Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)) combines these patterns.
The system maintains a pentesting task tree and uses reasoning,
generation, and parsing modules to propose next actions and interpret
outputs. The human is on the loop when monitoring the agent’s evolving
task tree and strategic recommendations. The human is in the loop when
executing commands in the target environment and feeding results back to
the agent.

#### 6.2.7. Agent self-improvement & learning

Agent self-improvement and learning describe whether a security agent
changes its behavior from feedback, examples, stored experience,
fine-tuning data, or reward-driven interaction. The identified learning
and adaptation mechanisms are summarized in
Table [10](#S6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 6.2.6. Agent workflow & orchestration ‣ 6.2. Survey Result: Approach ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment").

In-context adaptation. Learning from feedback within session refers to
improvement that happens inside the current task episode, without
necessarily changing model weights ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4);
[Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Saheed and Chukwuere,
2026](#bib.bib19); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Schüring et
al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59);
[Meruga, 2025](#bib.bib60); [Sharanarthi and Polineni,
2025](#bib.bib70); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). The feedback may come from tool output,
failed commands, execution traces, analyst observations, retrieved
evidence, peer-agent critique, or changes in the target environment. In
penetration testing, this usually looks like an agent trying a command,
reading the result, and adjusting the next step. Ginige et al.’s
AutoPentester ([Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)), for example, uses the
results of previous testing actions as context for later strategy
selection. Dai et al.’s RefPentester ([Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86))
makes the feedback loop more explicit by reflecting on failed operations
and using the result to guide subsequent penetration-testing stages.

Example-guided correction is a narrower form of in-context adaptation in
which the system uses examples, demonstrations, or corrected instances
to steer later outputs ([Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)). Schuring
et al. ([Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)) use this idea for
generating software-security learning materials: traceability links and
contextual examples help the agent refine generated educational content
so that it better aligns with security requirements. Here, the
correction signal is not a reward from an environment, but an example of
what a better output should resemble.

Cross-session learning. Storing successful trajectories preserves useful
interaction traces beyond a single run so that future tasks can reuse
solved strategies, action sequences, or reasoning patterns ([Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Happe et
al., 2026](#bib.bib63)). Zhuo et al.’s Cyber-Zero ([Zhuo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)) is an example. Instead of requiring access to the
original runtime environments, it reconstructs long-horizon
cybersecurity trajectories from public CTF writeups and simulated
personas, then uses those trajectories as reusable experience for
training cybersecurity agents.

Updating fine-tuning data carries improvement further by turning solved
trajectories, generated instructions, or adapted strategies into
training data for later model behavior ([Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40);
[Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)). In Cyber-Zero, Zhuo et al. ([Zhuo et
al., 2026](#bib.bib40)) use synthesized trajectories to train more
capable open-weight cybersecurity agents. Qin et al. ([Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)) describe a self-evolving security framework for 6G
space-air-ground integrated networks, where updated instruction data
helps the security-strategy generator adapt to changing or unknown
threats. In both cases, improvement is not confined to the current
prompt; the learning artifact is carried into later deployments or
training cycles.

RL-based improvement. Reward signal design defines what the agent should
optimize, such as API fault discovery, attack progress, service
preservation, threat mitigation, mission impact, or successful recovery
([Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2);
[Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Rigaki et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). Kim et
al.’s AutoRestTest ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) shows how reward
design can be tied directly to a software-security task: its API,
dependency, parameter, and value agents receive feedback from REST API
responses and use multi-agent reinforcement learning to coordinate
exploration and improve fault detection.

Environment-based RL uses a cyber range, simulator, network-security
game, or API-testing environment as the substrate for repeated
interaction and policy improvement ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2);
[Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Rigaki et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib73); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Loevenich
et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). Rigaki et al. ([Rigaki et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib81)) place LLM agents in network-security environments
and study their behavior under repeated prompt-exploit-observe cycles.
Loevenich et al. ([Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42)) assess
autonomous cyber-defense agents in a cyber-operations environment
against attacker strategies, combining DRL, augmented LLM components,
and knowledge-graph support.

### 6.3. Survey Result: Application

We analyze the surveyed LLM agents’ security applications along eleven
level-1 categories. Six of these—vulnerability detection & analysis,
exploit development & analysis, penetration testing & red-teaming,
vulnerability repair & hardening, intrusion & threat detection, incident
response, and threat intelligence & security operations (SecOps)—each
account for more than 10% of the surveyed papers and are presented with
individual taxonomy tables. The remaining lower-frequency
categories—fuzzing & test generation, malware analysis & detection,
reverse engineering, access control & authentication assessment, and
model attack generation & robustness evaluation—share a single table.
Within each category, we use the level-2 task groupings shown in the
corresponding table to organize the discussion.

#### 6.3.1. Vulnerability detection & analysis

This is one of the largest application areas in the taxonomy ([Kim et
al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Luo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib11); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62);
[Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68);
[Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Weber et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Sakib
and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Pendyala
and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)), as summarized in
Table [11](#S6.T11 "Table 11 ‣ 6.2.7. Agent self-improvement & learning ‣ 6.2. Survey Result: Approach ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment").
These agents support the discovery, localization, classification,
prioritization, and validation of vulnerabilities across source code,
smart contracts, binaries, APIs, and infrastructure configurations.

Vulnerability detection. Vulnerability detection refers to the
identification of security weaknesses in a given software artifact,
whether source code, bytecode, binary, or configuration file. In this
sub-task the agent inspects program entities, forms candidate
vulnerability hypotheses, and refines its assessment through tool use or
iterative reasoning ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Luo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib11); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Zemicheal
et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Yu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Weber et
al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97);
[Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99);
[Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)). Smart-contract auditing is
heavily represented in this sub-task ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6);
[Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Hu et
al., 2023](#bib.bib51); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). For example, GPTLens ([Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51)) decomposes auditing into a two-stage auditor/critic
process in which one agent proposes candidate weaknesses and another
suppresses false positives. LLM-SmartAudit ([Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)) extends this into a multi-agent conversational
architecture with a buffer-of-thought mechanism that propagates
intermediate insights across agents, while iAudit ([Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)) fine-tunes separate Detector and Reasoner models and
subjects candidates to a Ranker/Critic debate. General source-code
detection forms a second cluster ([Jie et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Yildiz
et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Jiao et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Sharanarthi
and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88);
[Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). DeepVulHunter ([Jiao et
al., 2025](#bib.bib41)) grounds multi-round reasoning in retrieval over
semantically similar code snippets, and JITVUL ([Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)) shows on a benchmark of 879 CVEs that ReAct-style
agents outperform raw prompting. Agent4Vul ([Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)) treats detection as an agentic code-analysis task in
which Commentator and Vectorizer agents reason over program context
rather than classify isolated snippets. A representative
repository-scale instance is RepoAudit ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88)),
which traverses interprocedural data-flow facts on demand and uses a
path-condition validator to suppress false positives, achieving 78.4%
precision at roughly \$2.54 per project. Binary and infrastructure
detection extends the sub-task beyond conventional source code ([Chen et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Weber et
al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89)).
ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)) detects vulnerabilities in
COTS binaries where no source is available, the IaC misconfiguration
agent ([Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57)) analyses
infrastructure-as-code definitions, and the multi-agent SQLi
pipeline ([Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)) targets deployed web
services.

API / input-surface security testing. This sub-task concerns testing for
vulnerabilities through external interfaces—APIs, web surfaces, network
endpoints, and infrastructure configurations—rather than by inspecting
source code alone ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Jiao et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib65); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Weber et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)).
AutoRestTest ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) decomposes REST API testing
into four cooperating agents trained via multi-agent reinforcement
learning, coordinating over a semantic dependency graph of API
operations. AutoPT ([Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22)) establishes an
end-to-end web-pentest benchmark and finds that agents are procedurally
fluent in the workflow but frequently fail to synthesise commands that
work against real targets. LLMSQLi ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65))
provides a black-box SQL injection detection tool driven by multi-agent
payload generation.

Zero-day discovery. Zero-day discovery refers to the identification of
previously-unknown vulnerabilities in realistic settings, as opposed to
classification of known weakness patterns ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)). For example,
AgentFuzz ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68)) reports 34 zero-day
vulnerabilities (23 CVEs assigned) across 20 popular open-source
LLM-agent applications, and PropertyGPT ([Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82)) discovers 12 zero-days in smart contracts through
retrieval-augmented formal property generation. BountyBench ([Zhang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)) instantiates 25 real-world systems with 40
monetary bug bounties and separate Detect/Exploit/Patch tasks, while
HPTSA ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)) exploits 14 real-world zero-day
vulnerabilities via a planner that dispatches specialist subagents.

Vulnerability localization. Vulnerability localization concerns
identifying the precise code regions responsible for a weakness, as
opposed to merely flagging a file or function as vulnerable ([Lbath et
al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74)). ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29))
localises bugs in binaries by combining an analyzer-friendly
intermediate representation with an LLM-friendly natural-language view,
then verifying candidates by constructing concrete triggering inputs.
PatchAgent ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)) performs fault localization
as the first stage of its repair loop, and AVIATOR ([Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23)) localises injection points when synthesising training
vulnerabilities.

Vulnerability classification. Vulnerability classification maps detected
findings to established taxonomies such as CWE types or CVSS severity
levels ([Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Zemicheal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). iAudit ([Ma et
al., 2025](#bib.bib34)) classifies smart-contract vulnerabilities
through its Ranker/Critic debate mechanism, the VEX-justification agent
of ([Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)) maps CVE observations to
impact categories across containerised environments, and
VulnPatch ([Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)) couples classification
with explanation and downstream patching.

Root cause analysis. Root cause analysis reconstructs the underlying
cause of a flaw rather than merely reporting its symptoms ([Aldaihan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Sakib and Khan,
2025](#bib.bib98)). Clouseau ([Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31))
traces attack chains back to root causes by autonomously traversing
system logs from a single point-of-interest. iAudit ([Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)) provides root-cause explanation through its Reasoner
agent, and VulnPatch ([Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)) generates
natural-language explanations of the vulnerability mechanism as part of
its detect-explain-patch pipeline.

Vulnerability prioritization / triage. Vulnerability prioritization
concerns ordering findings by severity, exploitability, or remediation
cost to guide effort ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74)). AgentFuzz ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68))
prioritises candidate taint-style findings by exploitability before
reporting them, and PatchAgent ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)) orders
localised faults to determine which to repair first within its
autonomous loop.

Bug triaging. Bug triaging refers to the assignment and routing of
detected findings to the appropriate remediation workflow ([Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)). LLM2Policy ([Chen et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib44)) routes configuration findings to the
corresponding policy layer, while PatchAgent ([Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74)) determines which findings are actionable within its
repair pipeline. This sub-task overlaps with prioritization but concerns
the routing decision rather than the ordering itself.

Vulnerability correlation. Vulnerability correlation links observations
across multiple data sources to build a coherent picture of a weakness
and its impact ([Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84)). PTGroup ([Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84)) correlates findings discovered across separate stages
of an engagement through chained prompt sequences, representing an early
form of cross-artifact vulnerability management.

#### 6.3.2. Exploit development & analysis

These agents, as summarized in
Table [12](#S6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ 6.3.1. Vulnerability detection & analysis ‣ 6.3. Survey Result: Application ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment"),
synthesise and analyse working exploits once a vulnerability is
known ([Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Loevenich et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Zemicheal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)). Much exploit-related activity is subsumed
by penetration testing; the papers here treat exploit synthesis or
analysis as a primary objective.

Exploit generation. Exploit generation concerns synthesising payloads or
scripts from vulnerability descriptions ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Adler et al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)). For example,
HPTSA ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)) dispatches specialist subagents
from a planning agent, achieving 4.3$`\times`$ improvement over
single-agent baselines on 14 real zero-day vulnerabilities. The study by
Happe et al. ([Adler et al., 2024](#bib.bib49)) compares five prompt
formulations for CVE-to-Metasploit-script generation across GPT-4o,
WhiteRabbitNeo, and Mistral in a military coalition-network context.

Payload crafting. Payload crafting refers to the construction of
concrete attack payloads that trigger the intended vulnerability
behaviour ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90)). In our corpus this sub-task is co-extensive with
exploit generation: every paper that synthesizes an exploit also
constructs a target-specific payload satisfying constraints such as
input filtering or memory layout. In general, the two remain distinct
capabilities, though.

Exploit chaining / attack-path construction. Exploit chaining concerns
assembling multi-step attack paths from individual vulnerability
primitives ([Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Loevenich et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib18); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58)). In these papers
agentic generative AI combines cybersecurity knowledge

steps.

Exploit detection. Exploit detection concerns identifying the presence
or feasibility of exploitable weaknesses from an external
perspective ([Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)).
VVF-AI ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99)) builds a proof-of-concept-based
verification framework to filter false-positive reports, and
ZT-ICAS ([Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)) uses agentic
scanning to detect exploitable weaknesses while hardening the scanner
itself against adversarial manipulation.

Exploit analysis / reverse engineering. Exploit analysis concerns
understanding the mechanism and impact of existing exploits ([Adler et
al., 2025](#bib.bib64)). Only one paper addresses this sub-task,
targeting the reverse engineering of exploits as a precursor to
developing defensive countermeasures.

interleaving reconnaissance, exploitation, and reporting ([Pendyala et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10);

Red team automation. Red team automation refers to the end-to-end
orchestration of adversarial campaigns in which the agent selects the
next action based on the current state of the engagement ([Pendyala et

2026](#bib.bib90)). For example, AutoPentester ([Ginige et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)) accepts only a target IP and iteratively invokes
standard security tools, outperforming PentestGPT by 27% in subtask
completion with substantially less human intervention.
PENTEST-AI ([Bianou and Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76)) structures attack
chains around MITRE ATT&CK, PTFusion ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83))
introduces a semi-decentralised multi-agent design with Model Context
Protocol–based tool invocation, and RefPentester ([Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86)) uses knowledge self-reflection to mitigate
hallucinated commands. The controller-based framework of ([Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35)) adds explicit workflow management to reduce
stage-skipping and token waste.
