frameworks incorporate reconnaissance as the initial phase. The
FOFA-based asset-search agent of ([Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89))
contributes context-aware reconnaissance queries over internet-exposed
assets, and the HPTSA planner ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)) performs
reconnaissance to inform specialist subagent dispatch.

Initial access. Initial access refers to the step where the agent gains
a first foothold in the target system ([Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20);
[Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22);
[Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Geng et al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Huang and
Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86)). In these papers the agent must translate
reconnaissance findings into a concrete exploitation attempt against a
live service. PenHeal ([Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75)) couples this
offensive phase with a remediation module via counterfactual prompting,
improving vulnerability coverage by 31% and reducing cost by 46%.

Full end-to-end pentest. These pentests require the agent to coordinate
the entire loop from initial probing through exploitation and, in some
cases, reporting or remediation ([Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige
et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Rigaki et
al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Geng et al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Huang and Zhu,
2024](#bib.bib75); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86)). The local-LLM study of ([Rigaki et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)) highlights the privacy, operational, and
reproducibility implications of deploying offensive agents without
cloud-hosted models, while CurriculumPT ([Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37))
organises the task as a curriculum that proceeds from easier to harder
targets and reuses stored experience across engagements.

CTF challenge solving. CTF challenge solving uses capture-the-flag
environments as controlled settings for studying offensive agent
capabilities ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Zou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69)). For example,
EnIGMA ([Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)) introduces Interactive
Agent Tools—a gdb-attached debugger and a persistent network client—that
let an LM agent drive genuinely interactive utilities, reaching
state-of-the-art results on 390 challenges across NYU CTF,
Intercode-CTF, and CyBench. CYBER-ZERO ([Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40))
synthesises agent trajectories from public writeups via persona-driven
simulation, CTFAgent ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)) uses a
plan-and-execute pattern with adaptive problem decomposition, and
CTFKnow ([Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69)) provides a 3,992-question
benchmark measuring technical CTF knowledge.

Privilege escalation. Privilege escalation concerns actions taken after
initial access to obtain higher-level permissions on the compromised
host ([Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79)).
hackingBuddyGPT ([Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63)) targets autonomous
Linux escalation, and Perses ([Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79)) tests
whether small local models can achieve escalation results comparable to
frontier models.

Lateral movement. This refers to an attacker’s traversal across a
network from one compromised host to others ([Rigaki et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86)). Only two papers
address this sub-task, both within broader end-to-end
penetration-testing frameworks rather than as a dedicated capability.

Exfiltration simulation. Exfiltration simulation concerns the
data-extraction phase of offensive operations ([Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26)).
AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)) includes
data-exfiltration objectives among its adversarial tasks. The sparsity
of work on lateral movement and exfiltration, and the absence of any
paper addressing persistence, indicate that post-access phases remain
substantially less developed than initial-access and reconnaissance
capabilities.

#### 6.3.4. Vulnerability repair & hardening

Agents in this category
(Table [14](#S6.T14 "Table 14 ‣ 6.3.3. Penetration testing & red-teaming ‣ 6.3. Survey Result: Application ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment"))
generate and validate patches and hardening modifications once a
vulnerability has been identified ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie
et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Samari et
al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68);
[Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98);
[Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)). Many of these papers also
appear under vulnerability detection & analysis, reflecting a common
detect-then-repair design.

Code review / auditing. Code review and auditing concern systematic
inspection of code for security weaknesses, often combining automated
detection with human-readable explanations ([Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51); [Sharanarthi and
Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98);
[Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)). This sub-task overlaps
substantially with detection, since identifying a weakness and reasoning
about how to remediate it are closely connected. The multi-agent
code-review framework of ([Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70))
integrates review, bug detection, and security analysis with a
FAISS-memory feedback mechanism, PropertyGPT ([Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82)) retrieves and adapts human-authored Certora
properties to produce verifiable invariants, and VulnGPT ([Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)) layers a controller-and-evaluator
AutoGPT loop on top of GPT-4.

Automated patch generation. Automated patch generation concerns
synthesising candidate fixes for identified vulnerabilities ([Zhang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Yu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Bouzenia
et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). For
example, PatchAgent ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)) integrates fault
localisation, patch synthesis, and test-suite validation into a single
autonomous loop, repairing over 90% of 178 real-world vulnerabilities
and outperforming specialised program-repair tools. VulnPatch ([Sakib
and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)) delegates detection, explanation, and patch
generation to three fine-tuned LLM agents, RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et
al., 2025](#bib.bib87)) interleaves test execution with fix synthesis,
and BountyBench ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)) contributes the
empirical finding that frontier agents are notably stronger at patching
than at exploitation.

Patch validation / verification. Patch validation concerns checking
whether a candidate fix actually resolves the targeted vulnerability
without introducing new problems ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Yu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Bouzenia et
al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). Validation
typically involves running the test suite, checking formal properties,
or executing candidates against proof-of-concept inputs. In
PropertyGPT ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)) verification is itself an
iterative agentic loop: the agent generates smart-contract properties
and then uses compilation, static analysis, and a prover to determine
whether they are usable.

Code hardening. Code hardening concerns preventive or structural changes
that reduce attack surface rather than targeting a specific
vulnerability ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Liu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)).
LLM2Policy ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44)) generates fine-grained
zero-trust policies from Kubernetes configurations, the IaC remediation
agent of ([Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57)) issues policy-level
recommendations for CI/CD pipelines, and the autonomous cloud agent
of ([G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55)) includes hardening among its
responsibilities.

Security policy enforcement. Security policy enforcement concerns
generating and applying rules that constrain system behaviour to meet
security requirements ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Liu et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)). LLM2Policy ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44))
and the IaC agent of ([Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57))
generate and enforce infrastructure-level policies, while
PropertyGPT ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)) enforces
formally-specified invariants as a policy layer over smart contracts.

with vulnerability detection & analysis as the largest category in the
taxonomy.

Log / traffic analysis & anomaly detection. This sub-task concerns
reasoning over runtime telemetry—logs, alerts, network flows, and packet
captures—to identify suspicious or anomalous patterns ([Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27);
[Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32);
[Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Qayyum et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59); [Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Zambare et
al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91); [Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). For example, Cognitive SOC ([Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)) deploys Triage, Enrichment, and StoryWeaver agents
that transform raw alerts into structured narratives where every claim
is linked to MITRE ATT&CK, Sigma, or CVE sources, achieving 99.6%
evidence linkage on 1,000 UNSW-NB15 alerts. The memory-augmented agent
of ([Saheed and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19)) provides IoT/IIoT anomaly
detection with edge-optimised SHAP explanations, NetMoniAI ([Zambare et
al., 2025](#bib.bib72)) deploys micro-agents at each network node for
local detection with central aggregation, and LaMA-SON ([Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)) introduces a self-evolving framework for 6G
space-air-ground integrated networks that updates its threat model as
new attack types appear.

Incident response automation. Incident response automation concerns
autonomous or semi-autonomous execution of defensive actions in response
to detected threats ([Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [De Santis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Mohammadi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib93); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). Autonomous
cyber-defence agents (ACDs) evaluated in CAGE-style
reinforcement-learning environments form a substantial cluster ([Towhid
et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42);
[Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Chowdhry et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Mohammadi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). The pure
LLM-based ACD of ([Mohammadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)) matches the
strongest RL agent submitted to CAGE-2 without retraining; hybrid
DRL+LLM architectures appear in ([Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42);
[Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Chowdhry et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)); and MARL+LLM blue/red training is explored
in ([Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). SOC orchestration forms the
second cluster ([Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92)). AutoBnB ([Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17)) compares centralised, decentralised, and hybrid agent
team structures for incident response using the Backdoors & Breaches
tabletop framework, and the agentic SOAR system of ([Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92)) replaces rigid no-code execution with LLM-driven
orchestration that interprets natural-language playbook descriptions and
branches dynamically on intermediate results.

Table 16. Paper attribution for Application: Threat intelligence &
security operations (SecOps)

Incident investigation. This task concerns the reconstruction of what
happened during or after a security event, including timeline recovery,
evidence assembly, and causal chain analysis ([Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17);
[Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [De Santis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Adler
et al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Zemicheal
et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Deng et
al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib93)). Clouseau ([Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31))
starts from a single point-of-interest and reconstructs attack chains
without prior training or predefined heuristics, achieving an average F1
of 99.78% across 21 scenarios including DARPA OpTC and ATLAS APT cases.
CFA-Bench ([De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)) provides a controlled
benchmark for evaluating investigation capability, and the workflow
of ([Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93)) automates first-stage triage
using structured queries over Suricata logs.

Attack attribution. This task concerns linking observed attack evidence
to a responsible actor, campaign, or technique ([Mei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57);
[Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66);
[Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77)). MAD-Agent ([Xenos et al.,
2025](#bib.bib66)) produces family-attribution reports via MCP-exposed
threat-intelligence tools, and CFA-Bench ([De Santis et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27)) benchmarks agent performance on attribution across
controlled scenarios.

Forensic analysis. Forensic analysis concerns the systematic collection,
preservation, and interpretation of digital evidence for post-incident
use ([De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Aldaihan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93)). CFA-Bench ([De
Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)) provides a controlled forensic
benchmark, Clouseau ([Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31)) performs
autonomous forensic investigation from a single seed event, and the
alert-investigation workflow of ([Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93))
assembles structured evidence for analyst review.

DDoS detection & mitigation. This sub-task concerns identifying and
responding to volumetric or protocol-level denial-of-service
attacks ([Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91)). LaMA-SON ([Qin et
al., 2025](#bib.bib16)) addresses DDoS within its self-evolving 6G
defence framework, the zero-trust SAGIN framework of ([Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48)) integrates detection into distributed network
defence, and the proactive cloud defence of ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91)) combines anomaly detection with automated mitigation.

Phishing & social-engineering detection. This sub-task concerns
detection of attacks that manipulate users through deceptive
communications or counterfeit interfaces ([Hmimou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95)). PhishAgent ([Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80))
combines online brand records with offline cached fingerprints and a
multimodal LLM to improve recall on novel brand-impersonation attacks,
and TrustNet ([Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95)) uses a hybrid
Random Forest and LLM-feature-characterisation pipeline for scam-website
detection, reporting 96.94% accuracy.

Alert triage. This concerns the initial classification and
prioritization of security alerts before deeper investigation ([Hmimou
et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93)). The
cross-domain multi-agent of ([Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3))
correlates email-verification, log-analysis, and IP-scanning agents
through a contextual-recommendation layer, achieving 93.6% detection
accuracy, and the workflow of ([Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93))
automates first-stage triage over Suricata logs.

Threat hunting. This refers to proactive, hypothesis-driven searching
for threats that evade automated detection ([Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92)). The agentic SOAR system of ([Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92)) supports proactive hunting by autonomously
orchestrating investigative playbooks over collected telemetry,
representing one of the few genuinely proactive defensive capabilities
in the surveyed corpus.

#### 6.3.6. Threat intelligence & security operations (SecOps)

Agents serving SecOps automate human-in-the-loop security workflows,
including threat-intelligence ingestion, reporting, policy generation,
and analyst support ([Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Sheikhi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Chen et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Cao et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Mohammadi
et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [G S et
al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57);
[Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66);
[Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86);
[Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91);
[Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Sakib and Khan,
2025](#bib.bib98)), as summarized in
Table [16](#S6.T16 "Table 16 ‣ 6.3.5. Intrusion & threat detection, incident response ‣ 6.3. Survey Result: Application ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment").

Threat intelligence synthesis. Threat intelligence synthesis concerns
the collection, correlation, and structuring of security information
from heterogeneous sources such as advisories, dark-web material, system
telemetry, and vulnerability reports ([Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3);
[Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5);
[Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16);
[Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Xenos et
al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Liu et
al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91); [Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). The cross-domain multi-agent of ([Hmimou et
al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) correlates email-verification, log-analysis, and
IP-scanning agents through a contextual-recommendation system, and the
trustworthy multi-LLM network of ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5))
addresses collaborative reasoning under adversarial-host risks using
blockchain-based audit trails and Byzantine Fault Tolerance consensus.

CTI analysis. CTI analysis concerns extracting indicators of compromise,
threat-actor tactics, and attack-chain structures from textual and
semi-structured intelligence sources ([Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3);
[Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Loevenich and Lopes,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Sheikhi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Xenos et
al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67)).
MAD-CTI ([Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67)) scrapes and classifies
dark-web sources—hacker forums, breach announcements, advisory posts—for
structured extraction, the CTI annotation system of ([Loevenich et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib18)) builds attack chains via cybersecurity knowledge
graphs, and Loevenich et al. ([Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42))
construct knowledge graphs from network logs, CTI reports, and
vulnerability frameworks to support autonomous cyber defence.

Security policy generation. Security policy generation concerns
translating natural-language security objectives or system
configurations into enforceable rules ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44);
[G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti,
2025](#bib.bib57); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91)). LLM2Policy ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44))
generates zero-trust policies from Kubernetes configurations, the IaC
agent of ([Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57)) issues policy-level
recommendations, the autonomous cloud agent of ([G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55)) includes policy generation among its duties, and the
proactive cloud defence of ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91)) translates
objectives into firewall rules.

Vulnerability report generation. Vulnerability report generation
concerns producing structured, human-readable reports from detection and
analysis outputs ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). The VEX-justification agent of ([Zemicheal et
al., 2024](#bib.bib62)) automates CVE impact analysis in containerised
environments via plan-and-execute LLM agents operating over SBOM,
source, and documentation, representing one of the earliest end-to-end
agentic vulnerability-management deployments.

Security Q&A assistant. Security Q&A assistants answer analyst or
learner queries by drawing on knowledge graphs, documentation, prior
incident records, or security curricula ([Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Schüring et
al., 2025](#bib.bib50)). The system of ([Schüring et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)) uses trace links and a multi-agent design to convert
real vulnerability scan results into contextualised security learning
materials, functioning as an interactive educational assistant.

CVE / advisory drafting. CVE and advisory drafting concerns producing
formal advisories from detection and classification outputs ([Wei et
al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). These
agents complement report generation with an output format suitable for
distribution through CVE or VEX channels.

#### 6.3.7. Other (Lower-frequency) security domains

The remaining application areas ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Lan and
Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8);
[Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11);
[Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Ning
et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29);
[Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Xenos et al.,
2025](#bib.bib66); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)) each
account for a small share of the corpus and are consolidated into a
single taxonomy table
(Table [17](#S6.T17 "Table 17 ‣ 6.3.6. Threat intelligence & security operations (SecOps) ‣ 6.3. Survey Result: Application ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment")).
They nonetheless indicate the breadth of emerging agentic security
applications beyond the dominant vulnerability-analysis and
offensive-security workflows.

Model attack generation & robustness evaluation. This category concerns
generating adversarial inputs against learned models and evaluating
their robustness ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et
al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Ayzenshteyn et
al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)). Jailbreak generation and prompt injection
generation / detection are addressed by the same four papers ([Zhang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Xu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)).
AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)) provides a dynamic
environment for evaluating prompt-injection attacks and defences, Agent
Security Bench ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8)) formalises attacks and
defences across 10 scenarios and 10 agents, and RedAgent ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib85)) is an autonomous context-aware red-teamer that
jailbreaks deployed LLM applications within five queries. Agent safety &
guardrail evaluation is the most represented sub-task here ([Zhang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et
al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Liu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)). ZT-ICAS ([Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100)) proposes zero-trust defence with input
neutralisation and capability-bounded tool invocation, and the deception
framework of ([Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) exploits LLM
biases and tokenisation quirks to cloak assets and lure attacking
agents. Adversarial example generation against ML/LLM components covers
attacks on non-agent learned models ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14); [Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56)). AgentPoison ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14))
demonstrates that poisoning a retrieval knowledge base compromises
downstream behaviour, CheatAgent ([Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28))
constructs black-box adversarial perturbations in user–recommender
dialogues, and AgentSA ([Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib56)) deploys LLM
user-agents with coherent fake personas for training-time shilling
attacks.

Fuzzing & test generation. This category concerns generating test inputs
that drive programs toward unexpected or security-relevant states ([Kim
et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96)). Test case generation
for security properties is the dominant sub-task ([Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96)): ConcoLLMic ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11)) uses an
LLM agent as a symboliser and natural-language constraint reasoner for
concolic execution, achieving 115–233% higher coverage than KLEE across
twelve real-world subjects, and MultiFuzz ([Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71)) couples dense retrieval over protocol RFCs with
multi-agent decomposition for network-protocol fuzzing. Smart seed
mutation appears in ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71)), symbolic execution guidance in ConcoLLMic ([Luo et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib11)), and crash triage & deduplication in ([Chen et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib44)). The absence of work on fuzzing harness
generation, seed input generation, and coverage-guided orchestration
indicates that agents are currently applied to the reasoning-heavy parts
of fuzzing rather than its infrastructure.

Reverse engineering. This category concerns recovering structure and
semantics from compiled artifacts or undocumented protocols ([Wael et
al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Abramovich et
al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96)). Disassembly & decompilation is addressed by three
papers ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Abramovich et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64)): ClearAgent ([Chen
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)) exposes both an analyzer-friendly
intermediate representation and an LLM-friendly natural-language view of
a binary, letting the agent form vulnerability hypotheses linguistically
and verify them by constructing concrete triggering inputs, and
EnIGMA ([Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)) supports binary reverse
engineering through Interactive Agent Tools in CTF settings. Protocol
reverse engineering appears in ([Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Wu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib96)), where FlowFSM ([Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15))
uses prompt chaining to extract finite-state machines from RFC documents
with reduced hallucinated transitions. Variable & type recovery is
addressed only by ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)).

Malware analysis & detection. This category concerns the analysis and
classification of malicious software ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)). Malware detection
is addressed by both papers ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7);
[Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)), while malware classification / family
attribution and malware behavior analysis appear only in
MAD-Agent ([Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)), which orchestrates static
analysis, dynamic sandbox analysis, and threat intelligence through
MCP-exposed tools. Anti-malware evasion analysis is addressed by
LAMLAD ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7)), which uses a
dual-agent manipulator/analyzer loop to perturb malicious Android APKs
while preserving functionality, achieving a 97% attack success rate in
an average of three queries. The absence of work on obfuscation
detection and malware generation marks this as the least developed area
in the corpus.

Access control & authentication assessment. This category concerns
evaluating whether access-control and authentication mechanisms are
correctly specified and enforced ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44)).
LLM2Policy ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44)) is the sole
representative, contributing to both firewall / ACL policy analysis and
access control policy generation / enforcement by extracting
microservice entity information from Kubernetes manifests and generating
fine-grained zero-trust access policies. The absence of any work on
authentication or authorization testing indicates that this domain
remains largely untouched by agentic approaches.

### 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment

#### 6.4.1. Metric

An assessment metric is an observable measure used to judge an agent’s
outcome, trajectory, safety, or comparative advantage. We organize the
reported measures into four attributes: task effectiveness, agentic
process/trajectory, safety/reliability, and comparative/baseline
evidence.

The tables use non-exclusive coding: a paper receives every attribute
directly supported by its assessment, so percentages within a table need
not sum to 100%. We audited the full text of every paper with a blank
row and retained a blank only when the paper reports no measure in that
table’s scope; the blank therefore means _unspecified for that
attribute_, not that the paper lacks an assessment altogether. After
this audit, six task-effectiveness rows remain blank: four
safety-focused studies ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Chen et
al., 2024](#bib.bib14)), Cognitive SOC’s process/report
assessment ([Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)), and an attack-chain
demonstration without a formal outcome metric ([Loevenich and Lopes,
2025](#bib.bib12)). Twenty-nine process rows remain blank because those
papers report outcomes without a trajectory measure, 70 safety rows
remain blank because the papers do not assess the agent’s boundedness or
adversarial reliability, and four comparative rows remain blank for the
specific reasons given below.

Task Effectiveness. Task effectiveness is the outcome-level attribute
that measures whether an agent accomplishes its intended security task,
such as finding a vulnerability, completing an exploit, producing a
valid patch, classifying an alert, or preserving service availability.
As shown in
Table [18](#S6.T18 "Table 18 ‣ 6.4.1. Metric ‣ 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment"),
the surveyed papers use ten task-metric families. Unlike
process-oriented metrics, these measures judge the result rather than
how the agent reasoned or used tools.

Accuracy and classification. Accuracy-oriented metrics are used when the
agent’s output can be judged against a discrete label, verdict, class,
or action. This family includes top-$`k`$ accuracy and CWE
classification for vulnerability

tasks, intrusion or log-detection accuracy, malware detection and family
classification, web/ phishing/scam classification accuracy, property or
exploitability verification accuracy, response-action accuracy,
asset-search accuracy, and investigation verdict accuracy. Such metrics
appear in papers on vulnerability detection, malware analysis,
phishing/scam detection, incident response, cloud operations, asset
discovery, command generation, forensics, CTF knowledge, and CTI
extraction ([Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95); [Lan and
Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13);
[Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [De Santis et
al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Jiao et
al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Qayyum et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Shah and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Ji et
al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). For example,
TrustNet ([Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95)) assesses a hybrid
machine-learning and multi-agent LLM detector for scam websites with the
standard classification suite of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1,
reporting that the LLM-agent team improves over the Random Forest
baseline on the labeled scam-detection task. In a different setting,
MAD-Agent ([Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)) treats malware analysis as
a combination of malware detection, behavior classification, family
attribution, and report generation, so task effectiveness is assessed
not only by whether the sample is detected but also by whether the agent
assigns the right behavioral interpretation.

Precision, recall, and F1. Precision, recall, and F1 are the dominant
metrics for detection-style tasks, especially vulnerability detection
and classification, intrusion detection, malware or phishing detection,
property generation, repository auditing, state-machine extraction, and
CTI analysis ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Saheed and Chukwuere,
2026](#bib.bib19); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Wael et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Yildiz et
al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Jiao et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59);
[Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Xenos et al.,
2025](#bib.bib66); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Liu
et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51); [Zemicheal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Huang and Zhu,
2024](#bib.bib75); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). These
metrics are useful when false alarms and missed findings have different
operational costs: precision reflects whether reported findings are
trustworthy, while recall or detection rate reflects whether important
security issues are being missed. Agent4Vul ([Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)), for instance, assesses a multi-agent smart-contract
vulnerability detector on more than 40,000 contracts and reports F1
improvements over 19 baselines across four vulnerability types.
PropertyGPT ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)) illustrates the same
family in formal-verification settings: it assesses generated
smart-contract properties using precision and recall against
ground-truth properties, and further reports how many known CVEs and
attack incidents are detected from the generated specifications.

Error rates. Error-rate metrics provide the complementary view of task
effectiveness by measuring how often the agent is wrong. Papers in this
group report false-positive rate, false-negative rate, RMSE/MAE, or
related error rates in vulnerability detection, intrusion detection,
recommender-system attacks, access-policy generation, and web-security
classification ([Saheed and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80); [Eilertsen et al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). These metrics matter because some
agentic systems are intended for analyst-facing use: a high
false-positive rate can overload analysts, while a high false-negative
rate can make an autonomous detector unsafe to rely on. For example,
vulnerability-detection papers that report false positives make clear
whether an agent is merely increasing the number of warnings or actually
improving the quality of surfaced findings; web and intrusion-detection
papers similarly use FP/FN rates to expose the tradeoff between
aggressive detection and operational noise.

Success and completion. Success and completion metrics are the largest
task-effectiveness family. They are used when a security task has an
executable or benchmark-defined endpoint, such as exploit or attack
success, CTF or penetration-testing completion, patch success, test
passing, remediation completion, or successful policy enforcement ([Luo
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Rigaki et
al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Geng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich et
al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et
al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57);
[Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Meruga, 2025](#bib.bib60); [Adler et
al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Sakib and Khan,
2025](#bib.bib98); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Rigaki et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib73); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Bianou and
Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). In offensive settings, success typically means
that the agent compromises the target, captures the flag, reaches the
vulnerable state, executes a proof-of-concept exploit, or achieves a
defined adversarial objective. CVE-Bench ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38)) is a representative example: it assesses agents
against real-world critical-severity CVEs in sandboxed web applications
and scores whether the agent can complete exploitation against a
reference target. BountyBench ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25))
broadens the idea by assessing detect, exploit, and patch tasks over
real bug-bounty issues, so completion is measured separately for
recognizing the bug, weaponizing it, and repairing it. In repair
settings, success is instead tied to whether the generated patch
applies, passes tests, and fixes the vulnerability;
RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87)) follows this pattern
by validating autonomous patches on Defects4J bugs and reporting
repaired-bug counts as the primary task outcome.

Findings and yield. Finding-yield metrics count the security artifacts
produced by an agent: valid bugs, confirmed vulnerabilities, captured
flags, CVEs, exploit chains, or bounty-relevant findings. This family
appears in work on penetration testing, exploit generation, formal
verification, vulnerability discovery, and security education or
challenge environments ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)). These metrics are
most informative when the task is exploratory and the target set is not
naturally reduced to a single label. For example, PropertyGPT ([Liu et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)) reports not only precision and recall for
generated formal properties, but also the number of known CVEs,
historical attack incidents, and zero-day bugs surfaced by the
agent-generated properties. This makes the assessment more
security-relevant than a pure classification score, because it connects
property generation to concrete vulnerability discovery.

Correctness and validity. Correctness and validity metrics ask whether
the produced artifact is semantically acceptable, executable, or
security-relevant. This family includes exploitability-verification
accuracy, attack-chain correctness, policy exact match, patch
correctness, test-pass or regression-preservation metrics, valid-test
ratios, and other validity checks for generated outputs ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Loevenich et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib18); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Bouzenia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib87); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). These metrics
are especially important for agentic systems that generate executable
artifacts, because a plausible-looking exploit, test case, policy, or
patch can still be invalid. MultiFuzz ([Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71)), for instance, assesses generated protocol-fuzzing
inputs in terms of their ability to exercise valid protocol behavior and
reach meaningful states rather than merely producing syntactically
varied messages. RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87))
similarly uses patch validation through compilation and tests, making
the metric about whether the agent’s edit actually repairs the program
rather than whether the proposed fix appears reasonable in natural
language.

Coverage. Coverage metrics measure how much of the target space the
agent explores. The surveyed papers use code coverage, branch coverage,
protocol-state or transition coverage, challenge-category coverage,
human-expert comparison, and other exploration-oriented measures ([Luo
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Segireddy,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)). This family is
common in fuzzing, testing, exploit exploration, and benchmark design,
where a single success outcome can hide shallow exploration.
MultiFuzz ([Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71)) provides a clear example:
it assesses whether a retrieval-augmented multi-agent fuzzer covers more
branches and protocol states than baselines such as NSFuzz, AFLNet, and
ChatAFL. In penetration-testing and challenge settings, category
coverage serves a related role by showing whether the agent can handle
diverse vulnerability classes rather than overfitting to one familiar
exploit pattern.

Time and responsiveness. Time-oriented task metrics measure whether the
agent completes a security task quickly enough for operational use.
Papers in this family report response time, latency, mean time to
respond or remediate, report-generation time, exploit time, and
asset-discovery speed ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Luo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib11); [Saheed and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Happe et
al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib91); [Hmimou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Liu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70);
[Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen
et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Cao et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Ismail et
al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)). These metrics
are particularly relevant for incident response, SOC automation, cloud
operations, malware analysis, network monitoring, vulnerability
analysis, and penetration testing, where a technically correct response
may still be ineffective if it arrives too late. For example, the
cloud-automation agent in ([G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55)) assesses mean
time to respond and remediation latency alongside accuracy and
policy-adherence metrics, reflecting the operational requirement that an
autonomous cloud-security agent detect an anomalous event, select an
action, and apply mitigation promptly. Similarly, MAD-Agent ([Xenos et
al., 2025](#bib.bib66)) reports the end-to-end time needed for tool use,
reasoning, and report generation, while NetMoniAI ([Zambare et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72)) measures detection latency under degraded links and
multi-node simulations.

Availability and reward. These metrics appear when security
effectiveness is measured by the state of an environment rather than by
a single prediction or generated artifact. They include cumulative
reward, mission or service availability, and defender-performance scores
in cyber-defense simulations and network-security games ([Towhid et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Mohammadi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43);
[Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). These metrics are useful for
defensive agents because the correct action is often not simply to block
every suspicious event; the agent must also preserve normal service. For
example, the CAGE-2 cyber-defense study ([Mohammadi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52)) assesses LLM-based defenders by balancing attacker
disruption against network functionality, which makes task effectiveness
a joint measure of security control and operational continuity. Other
simulation-based defender studies similarly use reward signals to
capture whether the agent’s sequence of actions improves the environment
state over time.

Qualitative and user assessment. Some papers assess task effectiveness
with expert judgments, user ratings, report-quality assessments, or
learning-gain measures ([Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Xenos et
al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Bianou and
Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). These
metrics are used when the output is difficult to reduce to a single
executable success condition, such as a security report, educational
artifact, analyst-facing explanation, or interactive penetration-testing
support. For example, MAD-Agent ([Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66))
includes report generation quality as part of malware-analysis
effectiveness, because a malware analyst needs a coherent account of
observed behavior and threat indicators rather than only a binary
malicious/benign label. PentestGPT ([Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)) is
another example: because the system is designed for interactive
penetration-testing assistance, user-facing usefulness and human
assessment complement task-completion metrics by capturing whether the
agent’s reasoning and recommendations are practically helpful.

Agentic process / trajectory. Agentic process and trajectory is the
attribute that assesses the path by which an agent reaches an outcome,
including its steps, tool calls, hallucinations, resource use,
iterations, intermediate artifacts, explanations, and economic value.
These metrics are particularly important because many security tasks are
long-horizon, tool-mediated, and partially observable. A final success
or failure score does not reveal whether the agent used tools correctly,
fabricated evidence, wasted iterations, produced a weak intermediate
artifact, or generated an auditable explanation.
Table [19](#S6.T19 "Table 19 ‣ 6.4.1. Metric ‣ 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment")
groups these process metrics into eight families.

Steps to completion. Step-based metrics measure how many actions,
subtasks, commands, or reasoning steps an agent needs before reaching a
task endpoint. They appear in penetration testing, software testing,
cyber-defense, vulnerability repair, fuzzing, and agent-security
benchmarks ([Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Ginige et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Towhid et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Meruga, 2025](#bib.bib60); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Debenedetti et
al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Rigaki et al., 2024a](#bib.bib73); [Rigaki et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84)). These metrics
are useful because two agents with the same final success rate may
differ substantially in operational efficiency and risk exposure: a
shorter trajectory may reduce cost and attack surface, while an
excessively short trajectory may indicate shallow exploration.
AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), for example,
assesses agents in stateful tool-calling tasks under adversarial data,
where progress through the environment matters because prompt injection
can alter not only the answer but also the sequence of tool calls. The
privilege-escalation study of ([Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63))
similarly records command counts and contrasts the trajectories of
autonomous agents with professional penetration testers.

Tool-call accuracy. Tool-call accuracy measures whether the agent
invokes the right tool, target, or environment operation for the current
task state. This metric is currently rare in the surveyed literature,
with CVE-Bench ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)) explicitly foregrounding
the need to assess agents that interact with sandboxed web applications
and execute attacks against concrete targets. The rarity is notable:
many security agents are advertised as tool-using systems, but most
assessments score only the final result. Tool-call accuracy gives a more
diagnostic signal by distinguishing reasoning failure from execution
failure, such as choosing an irrelevant scanner, issuing a malformed
command, or interacting with the wrong component of a web application.

Hallucination rate. Hallucination metrics measure unsupported claims,
fabricated evidence, invalid vulnerability explanations, or inconsistent
security reasoning in the agent trajectory. They are used in
vulnerability analysis, red teaming, SOC narrative generation, fuzzing,

auditing, and repair ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Chen et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib13); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Maklad et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98)). This family is
central for security agents because a hallucinated finding can become a
false alarm, an unsafe patch, or an incorrect incident narrative.
Cognitive SOC ([Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)) is a clear example:
it assesses evidence-backed security narratives with evidence linkage,
citation coverage, and hallucination rate, reporting a 0.1%
hallucination rate on 1,000 alerts while producing citation-backed
narratives. RepoAudit ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88)) attacks the same
problem in repository-level auditing by adding a validator that checks
data-flow facts and path-condition satisfiability before bug reports are
accepted, thereby treating hallucination mitigation as part of the agent
trajectory.

Cost and token efficiency. Cost and token-efficiency metrics measure the
resource burden of running an agent, including token usage, wall-clock
time, monetary cost, and assessment-time reductions. Papers in this
family study trajectory synthesis, CTF solving, SOC automation, cloud
operations, edge deployment, malware analysis, repository auditing,
program repair, fuzzing, and penetration testing ([Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et
al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Wei et
al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Mei et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich et
al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Qayyum et
al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70);
[Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen
et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Cao et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Huang and Zhu,
2024](#bib.bib75); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). These metrics
matter because many security workflows operate over large codebases,
long logs, interactive targets, or repeated benchmark trials.
CTFAgent ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)), for example, reports
interaction rounds, token volumes, and monetary cost per solved
challenge, while the privilege-escalation study of ([Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63)) reports token and dollar cost per exploited machine.
RepoAudit ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88)) gives a complementary
repository-scale example, reporting an average of 0.44 hours and \$2.54
per project while auditing real-world codebases.

Iteration count. Iteration-count metrics capture how many
revise-act-observe cycles, conversational turns, rounds, or repeated
attempts the agent needs. They appear in multi-step vulnerability
workflows, cyber-defense simulation, exploit or CTF tasks, program
repair, and agent orchestration studies ([Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36);
[Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Towhid
et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Weber et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79); [Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84)). Iteration counts are useful when the agent’s main
advantage is adaptivity: the assessment should show whether repeated
interaction actually helps or whether the agent is looping
unproductively. RepairAgent ([Bouzenia et al., 2025](#bib.bib87)) is
representative because the agent must propose a patch, validate it, and
use test feedback to revise the candidate; the number of iterations is
therefore tied to both efficiency and the quality of feedback use. In
offensive or challenge environments, the same metric distinguishes
agents that converge on a viable exploit path from agents that
repeatedly explore irrelevant actions.

Artifact correctness. Artifact-correctness metrics assess intermediate
or final artifacts produced by the trajectory, such as generated tests,
exploits, prompts, proofs, or analysis artifacts ([Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Loevenich et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib18)). This family differs from task success because it
asks whether a generated artifact is itself well-formed, executable, or
semantically faithful, even before measuring the downstream security
outcome. For agentic systems, this is an important diagnostic layer: an
exploit attempt can fail because the target is not vulnerable, or
because the generated artifact is invalid; a test can fail because it
reveals a bug, or because it is malformed. Artifact-correctness metrics
help separate these cases.

Report and explanation. Report and explanation metrics assess whether
the agent’s output is traceable, complete, understandable, and useful
for security practitioners. These metrics appear in papers on SOC
automation, incident response, vulnerability reporting, security
education, cloud operations, cyber-defense analysis, and auditing ([Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Schüring et
al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Ismail
et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98);
[Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). Cognitive SOC ([Sheikhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)) is again illustrative because it treats
evidence-backed narrative generation as the core output: the assessment
measures evidence linkage and citation coverage, not only
classification. In SOAR-style systems ([Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92)), explanation quality is similarly tied to operational
usefulness, because analysts need to understand why an investigation
verdict or response recommendation is justified before acting on it.

Economic and bounty value. Economic metrics map security outcomes to
monetary value, which can make benchmark progress more interpretable for
real-world vulnerability workflows. They are reported by
BountyBench ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)) and PropertyGPT ([Liu et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib82)). BountyBench assesses agents over real-world
bug-bounty systems and reports not only detect, exploit, and patch
success rates, but also dollar-valued outcomes derived from bounty
awards; PropertyGPT reports that a previously unknown bug found through
its generated properties received an \$8,256 bounty. This metric is
useful because two vulnerabilities with the same binary success label
may differ substantially in practical impact; dollar value provides a
coarse but concrete proxy for the economic importance of
agent-discovered or agent-repaired vulnerabilities.

Safety & reliability. Safety and reliability is the attribute that
measures whether the agent remains bounded and dependable under
adversarial inputs, repeated execution, prompt injection, poisoned
memory, or constrained operational settings. This group treats the agent
itself as part of the security boundary. As
Table [20](#S6.T20 "Table 20 ‣ 6.4.1. Metric ‣ 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment")
shows, seven metric families cover containment, robustness, consistency,
attack success, defense effectiveness, utility tradeoffs, and overhead.

Scope containment. Scope-containment metrics ask if the agent stays
within authorized goals, tools, data access, and execution boundaries.
They appear in work on jailbreak red teaming, zero-trust vulnerability
scanning, executable exploit benchmarks, prompt-injection-aware agents,
and constrained security workflows ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85);
[Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48)). These metrics are important because security agents
often interact with code, logs, metadata, web applications, or external
tools that may contain adversarial instructions. ZT-ICAS ([Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)) is a direct example: it designs agentic
vulnerability scanning around semantic input neutralization, ephemeral
context sharding, and capability-bounded tool invocation, then assesses
whether those constraints preserve analysis integrity when code comments
or dependency metadata are adversarially manipulated. CVE-Bench ([Zhu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib38)) complements this defensive view by recording
whether an exploiting agent takes actions outside the authorized target
scope.

Prompt-injection robustness. Prompt-injection robustness measures
whether the agent resists malicious instructions embedded in data, tool
outputs, retrieved documents, code comments, or environment state. It is
assessed in prompt-injection benchmarks, context-aware red teaming,
agentic scanners, and other tool-using security systems ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Zhang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)).
AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)) is a useful benchmark
example because it assesses agents that execute tools over untrusted
data with 97 realistic tasks and 629 security test cases. Its design
makes robustness observable through both utility checks and
attacker-goal checks over

the environment state. ZT-ICAS ([Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100)) addresses the same risk in code-security settings,
where adversarial comments and poisoned metadata can manipulate the
scanner’s reasoning.

Consistency. Consistency metrics assess whether repeated runs,
alternative prompts, inference budgets, or model configurations produce
stable security conclusions. Papers in this family apply repeated-run or
variance analysis to vulnerability detection, cyber defense, cloud
automation, remediation, network monitoring, penetration testing, and
prompt-injection-robust workflows ([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23);
[Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [De Santis et
al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Mohammadi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Zambare
et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Eilertsen
et al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62);
[Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). Consistency is a
reliability concern because security users need to know whether a
finding is robust or merely an artifact of stochastic generation.
VulnGPT ([Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)), for example,
repeats identical vulnerability queries, documents non-deterministic
findings, and assesses whether a self-reflection step changes those
conclusions. PTFusion ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83)) instead uses a
reasoning-similarity score across runs, while NetMoniAI ([Zambare et
al., 2025](#bib.bib72)) reports stable sub-five-second latency over
repeated tests.

Attack success rate. Attack success rate (ASR) is used when the
assessment is adversarial: the metric measures how often an attack
against the agent, model, recommender, or agent-mediated system
succeeds. This family includes jailbreaks, prompt injection, memory/RAG
poisoning, adversarial training data, recommender manipulation, and
agent red-teaming studies ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7);
[Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Ayzenshteyn et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). RedAgent ([Xu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib85)) assesses context-aware jailbreak generation
and reports that context-specific attacks substantially improve ASR
against customized LLM applications. AgentPoison ([Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)) studies a different attack surface: it poisons
long-term memory or RAG knowledge bases so triggered queries retrieve
malicious demonstrations, reporting high retrieval and end-to-end attack
success with very low poisoning rates. Together these papers show why
ASR is essential for agentic security assessment: attacks can target the
prompt, context, memory, retrieval layer, training data, recommendation
dialogue, or tool-mediated action path.

Defense success. Defense-success metrics measure whether a mitigation
reduces adversarial compromise while preserving useful behavior. They
appear in papers that assess defenses against jailbreaks, prompt
injection, memory poisoning, poisoned samples or training data, and
unsafe agent actions ([Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Lan
and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8);
[Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48);
[Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14);
[Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10)) provides a concrete example by comparing attacks and
defenses over stateful tool-calling tasks; in its initial environment,
deploying existing prompt-injection defenses reduces attack success but
does not eliminate the broader utility-security tension.
AgentPoison ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) assesses its attack under
perplexity filtering and query rephrasing, while LLM-SA ([Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48)) measures how accurately its analysis remains under
poisoning and the ACD-training study ([Loevenich et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib94)) defines poisoned-data and backdoor-trigger detection
rates for defensive training pipelines.

Utility-security tradeoff. Utility-security tradeoff metrics assess
whether robustness gains come at the cost of task completion or user
utility. This family is currently small but important ([Pendyala and
Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8);
[Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)). AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10))
explicitly motivates this tradeoff by assessing both user-task utility
and attacker-goal success over the same environment state.
AgentPoison ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) measures benign accuracy
alongside attack success, and ZT-ICAS ([Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100)) uses a utility-resilience test that penalizes
over-defensive behavior. These are stronger assessment patterns than
reporting defense success alone: an overly restrictive defense can
appear secure simply because the agent stops doing useful work.

Overhead. Overhead metrics measure the added cost of safety mechanisms,
such as latency, compute, token usage, or reduced throughput ([Pendyala
and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30);
[Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)). These metrics are necessary
because safety constraints are unlikely to be adopted in operational
security workflows if they impose prohibitive delay or cost.
ZT-ICAS ([Pendyala and Jeswani, 2026](#bib.bib100)), for example,
reports that its zero-trust constraints reduce analysis compromise with
manageable performance overhead, while the ACD-training
study ([Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)) explicitly includes the
compute and memory burden of robustness controls. This kind of
measurement is important because defended agents must still scale to
realistic codebases, networks, and security pipelines.

Comparative & baseline. Comparative and baseline is the attribute that
assesses an agent relative to traditional tools, prior learned methods,
a non-agent LLM, humans, other agent systems, or its own ablated
variants. These comparisons make raw task scores interpretable across
benchmarks, vulnerability classes, and target environments.
Table [21](#S6.T21 "Table 21 ‣ 6.4.1. Metric ‣ 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment")
groups them into six families. Four blank rows remain for papers that
provide no matching comparator—for example, a bench-

mark that compares attacks and defenses rather than agent
approaches ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8)), two assessments without a
conventional baseline ([Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Zambare et
al., 2025](#bib.bib72)), and a conceptual design study ([Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)).

Comparison with non-AI tools. The most common comparison is against
traditional security tools, program-analysis tools, fuzzers, scanners,
policy generators, runbooks, or other non-agent baselines ([Pendyala et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Loevenich and Lopes,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Wael et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Mei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [G S et al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Liu
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65)). These comparisons
clarify whether agentic behavior improves over established automation
rather than merely producing plausible natural-language output.
AutoRestTest ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) is a strong example: it
compares its multi-agent REST API tester against leading black-box REST
testing tools, including RESTler, EvoMaster, MoRest, and ARAT-RL, and
reports improvements in coverage and fault detection. ClearAgent ([Chen
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)) is instead counted under agent-system
comparisons because its reported baselines are CRAKEN and EnIGMA,
whereas VulnGPT ([Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)) directly
compares its scorecard with conventional SAST tools.

Comparison with prior ML/DL methods. Some papers compare agentic systems
with earlier machine-learning, deep-learning, reinforcement-learning, or
learned attack approaches ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zhuo
et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Jie et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Cao et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Shah and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Bouzenia
et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43);
[Rigaki et al., 2024a](#bib.bib73); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81)).
These comparisons are useful when the task was already studied before
LLM agents, such as intrusion detection, cyber-defense simulation,
vulnerability repair, CTF solving, or adversarial attack generation.
AgentPoison ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)), for example, compares
with four learned trigger-optimization and poisoning attacks, while
PatchAgent ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)) compares an end-to-end repair
agent with prior automated program repair methods.

Comparison with plain LLMs. Plain-LLM baselines hold the underlying
model family close to the agent under test but remove agentic
scaffolding such as iterative planning, memory, tool feedback, role
decomposition, or critic stages ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Qayyum et al.,
2025](#bib.bib59); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Huang and Zhu,
2024](#bib.bib75); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). They
provide the most direct evidence that a gain comes from the agent design
rather than from access to a stronger language model. For example, the
penetration-testing assessment in ([Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58))
compares its interactive architecture with a single-shot GPT-4 plan,
while VulnGPT ([Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)) contrasts
one-shot ChatGPT with the same models augmented by controller-driven
self-reflection.

Comparison with humans. Human baselines are used when the task is
traditionally performed by analysts, penetration testers, educators, CTF
participants, bug-bounty participants, or human system designers ([Zhang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Happe et
al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Segireddy,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Weber et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Zou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Bianou and
Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78)). These
comparisons are valuable but difficult to standardize because expertise
varies and human solutions often include tacit strategy not captured in
benchmark artifacts.
