dependency graph, LLM value generation, and reinforcement-learning
component; AgentPoison ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) disables each
loss term; and VulnGPT ([Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97))
contrasts one-shot analysis with its self-reflection stage. Such
ablations are important because the agent label can hide many
independent design choices.

#### 6.4.2. Dataset

An assessment dataset is the collection of subjects, environments,
tasks, or observations on which an agent is tested. We characterize
datasets by their origin, the security task they exercise, and
cross-cutting properties such as realism, label quality, scale,
modality, coverage, and accessibility. Dataset origin and security task
are integral attributes, so every paper has at least one supported
mapping in both tables. Within the characterisation table, however, a
blank cell means that the paper does not provide enough evidence for
that particular axis; we treat the information as _unspecified_ rather
than infer a label, scale, modality, or access condition.

Origin. Dataset origin is the attribute that records where assessed
subjects, environments, alerts, programs, or tasks come from: production
systems, competitions, threat feeds, curated public artifacts, or
controlled/generated sources. Origin determines whether an assessment
measures operationally realistic systems, reusable benchmark tasks,
adversarially controlled settings, or synthetic artifacts whose behavior
is easier to validate.

Table 22. Paper attribution for Assessment: Dataset origin

Real-world sources. Production systems are used when the assessment is
built from deployed services, realistic repositories, cloud
environments, bug-bounty systems, web applications, penetration-testing
targets, or other systems with operational structure ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90); [Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Yildiz et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Schüring et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib68); [Zambare et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Eilertsen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib93); [Ning et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Zemicheal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). These datasets are
valuable because agent behavior depends heavily on real system
structure: repository layout, service state, execution dependencies, and
operational constraints can all affect the agent’s trajectory.
BountyBench ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)) is representative
because it assesses agents on 25 real-world systems with bug-bounty
tasks that cover detection, exploitation, and patching. CVE-Bench ([Zhu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)) similarly grounds exploitation assessment in
vulnerable real-world web applications reproduced inside sandboxes.

Competition-derived datasets are common in offensive-security work,
especially CTF and cyber-range settings ([Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Abramovich
et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78)). These datasets offer well-defined success
conditions, reusable tasks, and rich community writeups, but they may
also reward puzzle-solving behavior that differs from real production
intrusion. ClearAgent ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29)), for example,
is assessed on binary challenges from NYU CTF Bench, while
Cyber-Zero ([Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)) leverages public CTF
writeups to synthesize long-horizon agent trajectories when the original
runtime environments are unavailable.

Threat feeds and security databases provide another real-world source,
including CVE/NVD data, vulnerability advisories and proof-of-concept
feeds, attack frameworks, threat-intelligence resources, and
incident-related feeds ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Loevenich and Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib13); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Yildiz et
al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Sheikhi
et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Shah and
Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Liu et
al., 2025d](#bib.bib89); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)). These sources
are useful for vulnerability classification, exploitability assessment,
SOC enrichment, and asset-discovery tasks because they connect agent
outputs to recognized security knowledge. For example, Cognitive
SOC ([Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)) enriches alerts with
threat-intelligence sources such as MITRE ATT&CK, Sigma rules, and CVE
databases, making dataset origin part of the evidence chain for
generated incident narratives.

Curated public artifacts include open-source repositories, malware
corpora, standards, benchmark applications, human-written properties,
and other reusable public collections ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11);
[Saheed and Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85);
[Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Lan and
Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15);
[Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29);
[Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Jiao
et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Xenos et
al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Bouzenia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib87); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98);
[Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)). This broader label avoids treating
public malware, RFCs, CTF writeups, prompts, or smart-contract
properties as software repositories. These datasets balance realism and
repeatability by retaining real artifacts while allowing researchers to
package, label, and rerun assessments.

Synthetic and controlled sources. Purpose-built programs and
environments are used when researchers need tight control over
vulnerabilities, attack paths, services, state transitions, or
agent-security tasks ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zhuo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95); [Hmimou et
al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Loevenich and
Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Liu,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Mei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Ginige et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Aldaihan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Towhid et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich
et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge
et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Cao et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi
et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [G S et
al., 2025](#bib.bib55); [Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57);
[Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64);
[Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Zambare et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Ismail et al.,
2025](#bib.bib92); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99); [Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Loevenich et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Rigaki et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib73); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Bianou and
Batogna, 2024](#bib.bib76); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et
al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)).
This is common in cyber-defense simulation, penetration-testing
benchmarks, adversarial-agent assessment, and controlled vulnerability
tasks. The advantage is measurability: the assessor can know the
intended flag, exploit condition, network state, or successful defense
outcome. The limitation is that the resulting task may underrepresent
the messiness of production systems.

Mutated corpora and generated variants are less common but important for
stress-testing coverage and robustness. Mutated corpora appear when
studies adversarially alter applications, contracts, inputs, or
retrieved content ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Samari
et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Maklad et
al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)). LLM-generated
datasets are used when a task requires scalable prompts, examples,
protocol models, negative samples, test inputs, or challenge-like
artifacts ([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Hmimou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69)). These are multi-label origins: e.g., CTFKnow ([Ji et
al., 2025](#bib.bib69)) generates questions from public competition
writeups and then filters and manually verifies them.

Dataset by security task. Dataset by security task is the attribute that
records the security capability an assessment exercises, such as
auditing, penetration testing, smart-contract analysis, repair, defense,
fuzzing, agent security, malware analysis, or SOC operations.

Table 23. Paper attribution for Assessment: Dataset by security task

This view distinguishes assessments that use similarly realistic
artifacts for different capabilities.
Table [23](#S6.T23 "Table 23 ‣ 6.4.2. Dataset ‣ 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment")
uses named benchmark families where possible and broader other-task
columns when a paper uses a task-relevant corpus outside those named
families.

Vulnerability detection & classification. Vulnerability-detection
datasets include named corpora such as BigVul, ReVeal, and
PrimeVul ([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Jiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41)), CVE/NVD-derived data ([Pendyala et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib13); [Loevenich et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib18); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [De Santis et
al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)), and other
vulnerability or audit corpora ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25);
[Toprani and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib57); [Sharanarthi and Polineni,
2025](#bib.bib70); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib88); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). The
broader other-audit column prevents custom Infrastructure-as-Code,
repository, PoC, and benchmark collections from being left unmapped
merely because they do not use one of the three named corpora.

Penetration testing & CTF. Penetration-testing and CTF datasets cover
InterCode-CTF ([Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Abramovich et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69)), PicoCTF ([Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69)), HackTheBox ([Ginige
et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78)), VulnHub ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Mei et
al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Deng et al., 2024](#bib.bib78); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84)), AutoAttacker-style benchmarks ([Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37); [Thanh et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Weber et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Dai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75)), and other custom
pentest or CTF suites ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Happe et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63); [Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib90); [Loevenich and Lopes,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Adler et al., 2024](#bib.bib49); [Zou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib65); [Bianou and Batogna,
2024](#bib.bib76); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib84)). These datasets are
well suited to long-horizon assessment because the agent must gather
evidence, choose tools, execute actions, and adapt to observations. A
paper may legitimately receive both a named-benchmark and an
other-pentest mark when it is assessed across multiple suites.

Smart contracts. Smart-contract datasets form a distinct application
domain spanning contract vulnerability detection, auditing, and property
verification ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Yildiz et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Hu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51)). This attribute was added because these eight papers
previously had no integral task-domain column even though their datasets
and assessment targets were explicit.

Web, phishing, and scam. Web, phishing, and scam datasets assess whether
agents can identify malicious sites, web threats, or scam
behavior ([Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95); [Cao et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib80)). TrustNet ([Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95)),
for example, assesses a hybrid ML and LLM-agent detector for scam
websites using labeled examples and standard classification metrics.
This category differs from CVE exploitation because the task is often
judgment or classification over web-facing evidence, not interaction
with a vulnerable application.

Repair and bug-fix. Repair datasets assess whether agents can modify
code correctly, usually with tests, proof-of-concept inputs, or known
bug labels ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Toprani and Madisetti,
2025](#bib.bib57); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Bouzenia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib87)). PatchAgent ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74)) uses
real-world vulnerability cases with proof-of-concept tests and
functional test suites, while BountyBench ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25)) couples repair with detection and exploitation
tasks; its multiple task marks therefore reflect a genuinely multi-task
benchmark.

Cyber defense and simulation. Cyber-defense datasets and environments
support defender agents, network-security games, attack-defense
simulations, and autonomous response assessment ([Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib5); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Towhid et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Loevenich
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib43); [Rigaki et al., 2024a](#bib.bib73); [Rigaki
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94)).
These datasets often define stateful environments where the agent must
preserve service availability while detecting or mitigating an attacker.
The CAGE-2 study ([Mohammadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)) is
representative because it assesses LLM-based cyber defenders in a
simulated network environment where reward reflects both security and
operational continuity.

Security testing and fuzzing. Security-testing datasets cover REST API
and program-level testing as well as RFC-derived protocol models and
fuzzing targets ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Wael et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71)).
MultiFuzz ([Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71)) uses RFC-derived knowledge
for protocol exploration, whereas AutoRestTest ([Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)) assesses graph- and agent-guided REST API input
generation. The broadened label records the shared testing objective
without incorrectly describing every assessment as protocol fuzzing.

AI and agent security. AI- and agent-security datasets assess prompt
injection, jailbreaks, memory poisoning, unsafe tool use, taint-style
agent vulnerabilities, and attacks on other learned systems ([Gu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Pendyala and Jeswani,
2026](#bib.bib100); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8); [Ayzenshteyn et
al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Debenedetti et
al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)). AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10))
provides realistic tool-calling tasks with prompt-injection tests, while
AgentFuzz ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68)) targets vulnerabilities in
LLM applications and ([Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Ning et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)) assess agent-generated attacks on recommender
systems.

Asset discovery and OSINT. Asset-discovery and OSINT datasets assess
whether an agent can search, correlate, or prioritize exposed assets and
vulnerability-relevant information ([Liu et al., 2025d](#bib.bib89)).
This category is small in the current taxonomy, but it is practically
important as many security workflows begin with asset visibility rather
than code or exploit generation. Dataset design in this category needs
to capture both retrieval accuracy and the operational speed of
discovery.

Malware and Android apps. Malware and Android-app datasets support
agentic analysis of suspicious software, app behavior, family
attribution, or malware reports ([Lan and Nait-Abdesselam,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)). MAD-Agent ([Xenos
et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)) illustrates this task family by combining
static and dynamic analysis tools with threat-intelligence access, then
assessing detection, behavioral classification, family attribution, and
report quality. Compared with vulnerability datasets, malware datasets
often require interpreting multiple evidence streams rather than only
matching a code location to a vulnerability label.

Intrusion, SOC, and SOAR. This broader family covers intrusion or
traffic detection as well as alert triage, enrichment, reporting,
response recommendation, and automated investigation ([Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [Aldaihan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [G S et al.,
2025](#bib.bib55); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Meruga,
2025](#bib.bib60); [Shah and Madisetti, 2025](#bib.bib67); [Zambare et
al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)). Cognitive
SOC ([Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)) assesses evidence linkage,
citation coverage, hallucination, and time-to-recommendation on 1,000
alerts. The broader label prevents intrusion datasets from being
excluded merely because they are not packaged as SOC alerts.

Other security tasks. The residual task category is used for two
explicit but otherwise uncovered assessment targets: cloud-native
access-control policy generation ([Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44)) and
context-aware software-security education ([Schüring et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)). It is not an unknown or unspecified label; it
records a defined task that falls outside the listed families.

Dataset characterisation axes. Dataset characterisation axes are
cross-cutting attributes of the assessment data: realism, label quality,
scale, artifact type, vulnerability-type coverage, and accessibility.

Table 24. Paper attribution for Assessment: Dataset characterisation
axes

These axes explain why results may not be directly comparable even for
the same application.
Table [24](#S6.T24 "Table 24 ‣ 6.4.2. Dataset ‣ 6.4. Survey Result: Assessment ‣ 6. Paper Attribution ‣ LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: Approaches, Applications, and Assessment")
applies every supported item to each paper; multiple checkmarks are
therefore expected when an assessment combines modalities or access
conditions. Realism and scale are coded at the level of the assessed
collection, while unsupported or unreported axis values remain blank and
are interpreted as unspecified.

Realism. The surveyed datasets span fully synthetic, semi-synthetic, and
fully real-world settings. Fully synthetic datasets are used when the
authors construct all or most of the assessed artifacts or environment
states ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Gu et al., 2026](#bib.bib56);
[Liu, 2025](#bib.bib17); [Samari et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Thanh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)). Semi-synthetic datasets combine real
components with controlled modifications, generated tasks, simulated
environments, or benchmark wrappers ([Pendyala et al., 2026](#bib.bib4);
[Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26);
[Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40);

2023](#bib.bib51)). The tradeoff is consistent across the survey:
real-world datasets improve ecological validity, while synthetic and
semi-synthetic datasets improve control, repeatability, and safety.

Label quality. Label quality determines whether the assessment target is
trustworthy. Some datasets rely on automated labels, such as generated
labels, oracle checks, or test-derived labels ([Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)).
Competition-verified labels appear in CTF and cyber-range datasets where
a flag, official solution, or challenge infrastructure validates
success ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Ayzenshteyn et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30); [Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Abramovich et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45); [Segireddy, 2025](#bib.bib58); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Shen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)).
Expert/reference-verified labels are grounded in official behavior,
human-written references, manual annotation, or review by domain or
security experts ([Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Lbath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Samari et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Adler et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Zemicheal et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Xenos et al.,
2025](#bib.bib66); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Cao et al., 2025a](#bib.bib80); [Liu et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib82); [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Eberhardt and
Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Sakib and Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Liu
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99)). Noisy or weak labels appear when large
vulnerability corpora or generated benchmark artifacts may contain
imperfect ground truth ([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Segireddy,
2025](#bib.bib58)). When no evidence supports one of these label
sources, the label-quality value is left unspecified rather than
guessed.

Scale. Dataset scale varies widely. Small datasets are common in
expensive, environment-heavy assessments such as CTF, cyber-defense,
malware analysis, policy generation, and exploit benchmarks ([Chen et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Zhuo et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Loevenich et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich
et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Chowdhry et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Adler
et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Xenos et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)).
Medium-scale datasets appear in phishing, vulnerability, SOC,
prompt-injection, and CTF-knowledge assessment ([Abdelhamid et al.,
2026](#bib.bib95); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8); [Sheikhi et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Eberhardt
and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib99)).
Large datasets are relatively rare in the verified taxonomy and appear
mainly in large vulnerability-detection corpora and smart-contract
analysis ([Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)). This imbalance reflects a core assessment challenge:
agentic security tasks are often costly to execute because they require
live environments, tool interaction, sandboxing, or human validation, so
scale is often traded for realism and measurement depth.

Language and artifact type. Some datasets are single-language code
datasets, which are common in vulnerability detection, smart-contract
analysis, repair, and formal-verification tasks ([Luo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib11); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Jie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Ma et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Toprani and Madisetti,
2025](#bib.bib57); [Sharanarthi and Polineni, 2025](#bib.bib70); [Yu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib74); [Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib82); [Sakib and
Khan, 2025](#bib.bib98); [Eberhardt and Milánkovich, 2024](#bib.bib97)).
Others involve binary or compiled artifacts, including malware, reverse
engineering, CTF binaries, and exploit-development tasks ([Zou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Lan and Nait-Abdesselam, 2025](#bib.bib7); [Jie et
al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib29); [Abramovich et
al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Adler et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Xenos et al.,
2025](#bib.bib66)). The largest artifact family is network/log data,
which appears in cyber-defense, intrusion detection, protocol fuzzing,
penetration testing, SOC alerting, and web-security tasks ([Pendyala et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib5); [Saheed and
Chukwuere, 2026](#bib.bib19); [Rigaki et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zou et
al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib83); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib91); [Abdelhamid et al., 2026](#bib.bib95); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib96); [Hmimou et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Loevenich and
Lopes, 2025](#bib.bib12); [Wael et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Qin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Loevenich et al., 2025b](#bib.bib18); [Mei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [De Santis et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Ayzenshteyn et
al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Aldaihan et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Sheikhi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Towhid et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Loevenich et al., 2025a](#bib.bib42); [Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib44); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Chowdhry et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Kluge et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Cao et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib48); [Mohammadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib52); [Qayyum et
al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Honnalli and Farooq, 2025](#bib.bib61); [Adler
et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Ji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib69); [Maklad et al., 2025](#bib.bib71); [Zambare et al.,
2025](#bib.bib72); [Dai et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Liu et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib89); [Ismail et al., 2025](#bib.bib92); [Eilertsen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib93); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Loevenich et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib43); [Zou et al., 2024](#bib.bib53); [Rigaki et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib73); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib84); [Loevenich et al., 2024a](#bib.bib94); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99)). Artifact type strongly shapes the agent’s required
capabilities: code datasets emphasize semantic program reasoning, binary
datasets require lower-level analysis, and network/log datasets
emphasize temporal correlation and environment state.

Vulnerability type coverage. Some datasets explicitly cover multiple
vulnerability classes, attack types, or benchmark categories ([Zhang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Happe et al., 2026](#bib.bib63); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib29); [Ayzenshteyn et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Geng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib35); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Abramovich et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Segireddy,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Qayyum et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Adler et al.,
2025](#bib.bib64); [Ji et al., 2025](#bib.bib69); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib74); [Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Zou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53); [Huang and Zhu, 2024](#bib.bib75); [Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78); [Rigaki et al., 2024b](#bib.bib81); [Liu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib99)). Coverage matters because many agents perform well
on familiar vulnerability patterns but fail when the target requires a
different exploitation strategy, input modality, or repair mechanism.
BountyBench ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib25)) is illustrative because
it spans real bug-bounty vulnerabilities across OWASP risk categories
and assesses detect, exploit, and patch tasks. PentestGPT ([Deng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78)) similarly uses targets that cover OWASP top-10
vulnerabilities and multiple CWE items, making subtask performance more
informative than a single aggregate score.

Accessibility. Accessibility determines whether assessment results can
be reproduced. Fully public datasets are the dominant accessibility
category ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib11); [Saheed and Chukwuere,
2026](#bib.bib19); [Lbath et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib25); [Zou et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhuo et al.,
